resources.string: A simplified view of a normal continuous blood capillary in tissue. Exchange varies by tissue; paths, sizes and timing are not to scale. For education, not medical advice.
A lining between blood and tissue
A thin layer of endothelial cells lines the capillary. It forms a selective boundary between the lumen, where blood flows, and the interstitium, the space around tissue cells.
In many tissues, the balance of pressures lets some water filter from the blood into the tissue space. This outward flow is called filtration.
Small dissolved substances can diffuse across the lining in either direction. The net movement of each solute is from higher to lower concentration. This is not bulk fluid flow.
Larger molecules mostly stay in blood
Many large molecules, such as the plasma protein albumin, cross less readily than small solutes. Most albumin stays in the blood as it passes through, but some can cross.
Excess fluid from the tissue space enters nearby lymphatic capillaries. Once inside, it is called lymph. This route does not depend on ongoing fluid uptake at the venous end of the blood capillary.
